To look with more statistical power, we also conducted analyses in functionally defined regions of interest (ROIs) along the lateral stream. The learned dimensions explained more variance than the annotations in all lateral regions (Extended Data Fig. 8). The advantage was largest in EVC, MT and EBA (∆r2 ≈ 0.2) and substantial in pSTS (∆r2 ≈ 0.18), but small in anterior STS (aSTS; ≈ 0.04), where the two models performed comparably and both remained well below the noise ceiling. Finally, to understand how individual dimensions relate to responses across the visual cortex, we performed a winner-take-all searchlight analysis in which each voxel was labeled by the dimension (among the top 11) whose similarity structure correlated most strongly with the local neural RSM (Extended Data Fig. 9). The best-predicting dimension varied across cortex, indicating that different regions are aligned with different aspects of the learned geometry.

3 Discussion

Here we characterized the mental representations of dynamic social scenes directly from behavior, by learning an interpretable embedding to predict similarity judgments of naturalistic two person videos. The embedding explained roughly twice as much behavioral variance as pre-labeled annotations derived from prior theories, and absorbed most of the variance the annotations explained. Critically, these dimensions fractionate content that broad semantic categories and pre-labeled annotations collapse: infant-related scenes separated into caregiving, crying, and affectionate play rather than forming a single "baby" category. Similarly, scenes depicting "play" are separated based on the participants and their social relationship (child-child versus parent-child). The same dimensions predicted the representational geometry of the visual cortex, including the lateral pathway, better than the pre-labeled annotations, in fMRI data where participants passively viewed the videos, extending the significance of these dimensions beyond similarity judgments. Together these results reveal a fine-grained organization of natural social scenes, combining social relationships and actions, that is shared across behavioral judgments and neural representations. These results extend the data-driven embedding approach from static objects [17, 22] and isolated actions [20, 21, 27, 28] to dynamic, two-person interaction video clips. Prior work aimed at recovering the organizing dimensions of action representation more generally has uncovered relatively coarse social semantic, and action-related categories. By focusing on two-person interactions, we identified nuanced distinctions among social events. The fact that learned dimensions blend information about actions and social relationships highlights the importance of the underlying event structure and thematic roles (i.e., who did what to whom). Such event role representations are central to human language, and recent work has highlighted their importance in visual narratives [29] and recent work suggests forms of this structure may be embedded in visual perception [10, 30] . This joint specification is not captured by trait axes, which describe relationships without activities, nor by action categories, which describe activities without relationships.

The short, de-contextualized nature of the video clips used may have emphasized a more visual or action-based feature space for participants [8] . However, features describing social relationships, namely intimacy and dominance, were the pre-annotated features that best predicted similarity judgments. In the learned embeddings, these social-affective features were distributed across multiple dimensions, both positively and negatively (intimacy for example distinguished adult conversation versus caregiving and infant-play dimensions). Surprisingly, action-related features were not strong standalone predictors of human similarity or the learned dimensions. Even the full set of pre-labeled annotations based on prior action-based theories [6, 7, 12] was largely not predictive of the similarity space or learned embeddings. Remarkably, the learned dimensions also matched neural data better than these action-based features, even in the lateral stream. These findings are consistent with prior studies showing that lateral occipital regions correspond to behaviorally derived semantic structure [31, 32] , which suggest that information about social relationships may play a more important role in these regions than originally anticipated [8, 11, 13] . Unlike other visual pathways, these lateral stream regions have also been difficult to predict with trained deep-network models [33] , underscoring that these behaviorally derived dimensions capture structure that current image-computable models cannot.

The learned dimensions are interpretable and reproducible (Extended Data Fig. 2), but one limitation is that their labels are based on video caption analysis and visual inspection. Thus, an important open question is whether and how these features can be derived in a bottom-up, a priori manner. Future work could collect participants' ratings for each dimension, as seen in prior work for objects [17] , to provide new taxonomies for social interactions. Recent work has also shown that with fine-tuning, video foundation models can learn to reproduce this human social similarity structure [34] , suggesting a path forward for annotating new videos in an image-computable way. Future work should test whether and how these approaches generalize to a wider set of new videos to see how these learned dimensions generalize across social contexts, populations, and stimulus sets.

Together, these findings show that the similarity structure of social scenes is highly nuanced and fine-grained, organized around novel combinations of actions and social relationships not captured by prior social-affective or action-based theories. This work provides a compact set of behaviorally derived and neurally relevant dimensions for future studies of social representations in adults, throughout development, and in AI systems. More generally, it provides a framework to extend data-driven representational spaces to increasingly complex and naturalistic social settings.

4 Methods

4.1 Participants and stimuli

The stimulus set contained 250 short video clips (3 seconds each) displaying naturalistic social interactions [12] . The selected clips came from the Moments in Time dataset [5] . The aim of this selection was to enforce a requirement of two-person interactions across varying relationship types (e.g., friends, strangers, parent-child), activities (e.g., conversation, playing, eating, task collaboration), emotional tone (e.g., friendly, adversarial, neutral), and setting (indoors vs. outdoors; private vs. public spaces). The stimuli contained no audio to eliminate cues related to spoken language.

Participants totaled N = 232, recruited from an online university crowd-sourcing platform and were awarded course credits for participation. The triplet odd-oneout experiment was hosted and collected similarity judgments through the Meadows Research platform (https://meadows-research.com). All participants gave informed consent, and data was collected under the JHU Homewood Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval.

In addition to the similarity judgments, captions describing each video were previously collected from a different set of participants, which we use to facilitate content and learned dimension analysis.

4.2 Triplet odd-one-out similarity task

Each participant completed a set of at least 220 trials in which three videos were simultaneously presented in a random arrangement on a web-based interface. The instruction for each trial was "From each triplet, please choose the one you feel is the odd-one-out.". This forced-choice paradigm reveals perceptual similarity structure by indicating which two of the three stimuli are judged as most alike [17, 35] . Two sets of participants and trials were collected: 215 participants judged 49,484 triplets of the 250 videos used as a training and validation set. 17 additional participants judged 3,739 triplets of a 50 video subset (pre-determined test stimuli), used for held-out evaluation.

Only a small fraction of possible triplets can be sampled (49,484 of 2,573,000 for 250 videos; 3,739 of 19,600 for 50 videos), so triplets were chosen using a greedy setcover selection algorithm [34] to cover pairs rather than triplets: every pair of videos co-occurs in at least one triplet, with on average ∼4 judgments per pair in the training set and ∼9 in the test set. Unlike probabilistic random sampling [17] , this achieves complete pairwise coverage at a smaller triplet count. This was a deliberate design trade that maximizes reliable RSM estimation per judgment for a stimulus set of this size.

Each set of trials included catch trials in which one video appeared twice alongside a different video; the correct response was the non-repeated video. Participants who selected the repeated video on any catch trial were excluded from all analyses (n = 30). The final sample had a mean age of 19.5 years; 148 participants identified as female, 76 as male, 2 as non-binary, and 6 did not report gender. In terms of ethnicity, 78.0% identified as not Hispanic or Latino and 19.0% as Hispanic or Latino, with 3% not reporting ethnicity. In terms of race, 39.2% identified as Asian, 36.2% as White, 10.8% as Black, 4.7% as more than one race, 3.9% as other, and 0.4% as American Indian, with 4.7% not reporting race.

A Representational Similarity Matrix (RSM) was created using the pairwise judgments from the collected held-out triplets utilizing the probabilities of choices and the counts of judged pairs. In reporting we utilize a split-half reliability metric to estimate the noise ceiling of the human judgments. Specifically, we randomly split the triplet judgments into two halves, construct a separate representational similarity matrix (RSM) from each half, and compute the Spearman correlation between the upper triangles of the two RSMs (restricted to pairs with at least one observation in both halves). This procedure is repeated over 1,000 random splits and the mean half-length correlation is corrected using the Spearman-Brown corrected formula, r SB = 2r/(1 + r), to estimate the reliability of the held-out dataset. The resulting value serves as a noise ceiling, representing the maximum correlation any model could be expected to achieve given the variability in human responses.

4.3 Computational embedding model

To model the mental representation of the videos, we trained a sparse positive similarity embedding (SPoSE) [17] model optimized to predict the triplet choices observed in human participants. The model represents each video as a non-negative point in a D-dimensional space, initially set to D = 90 as an overcomplete basis. We employed a triplet-loss learning method similar to that described by Hebart et al [17].

For a triplet (i, j, k), the similarity of each pair was defined as the dot product of their embedding vectors. The probability that a given pair was judged most similar, with the remaining video as the odd one out, was the softmax of the three pairwise similarities. The model was trained to minimize the negative log-likelihood of the human choices, plus an L1 penalty on the embedding weights to promote sparsity (λ = 0.01). The penalty was ramped up linearly from 0 to its full value over the first 20 epochs, which lets the embedding first fit the choice data before sparsity is imposed.

Optimization used Adam (learning rate = 0.001, β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999, ϵ = 10 -7 ) with a mini-batch size of 100 triplets, and the training data were reshuffled every epoch. The triplet dataset was split at random at the triplet level: 90% of judgments (44,535) were used for training and 10% (4,949) for validation. Training ran for at most 200 epochs, with early stopping when validation accuracy did not improve by at least 0.0005 for 20 consecutive epochs. After training, dimensions were pruned following Hebart et al. [17] : any dimension whose maximum activation across all 250 videos was below 0.1 was removed. This left 40 dimensions.

Top dimension selection used only training-set 10-fold cross-validated r 2 ; the Kneedle elbow [26] was identified on this training curve and fixed before any evaluation of the held-out test RSM. Of the pruned 40 dimensions, approximately 11 were identified as a core interpretable subset that best explains the similarity judgments, as described in the Results. All primary analyses, including the explained variance of human similarity judgments and neural comparisons, use the full 40-dimension embedding, unless otherwise stated, while the top 11 dimensions are used for visualization and interpretability.

4.4 Pre-labeled annotations

We used the twelve pre-labeled annotations released with the stimulus set [12] : spatial expanse, indoor/outdoor, inter-agent distance, agents facing, object-directed action, acting jointly, communication, cooperation, dominance, intimacy, valence and arousal. Each continuous feature was rated by at least 10 online participants per video on a five-point Likert scale and averaged across raters; indoor/outdoor is a binary label. For each feature we built an RSM over the test videos whose entries are one minus the Euclidean distance. Rater reliability for these annotations is reported in McMahon et al [12] . A thirteenth, action-category RSM was built from each video's Moments in Time label, with two videos counted as similar if they share a category, 0 otherwise.

4.5 Multiple linear regression RSA

To evaluate pre-labeled annotations and learned dimensions, we constructed models predicting similarity using multiple regression RSA [24, 25] . Predictors (13 annotation RSMs, or the 40 and top 11 dimension similarity vectors) were entered into an ordinary-least-squares regression predicting the upper triangle of the held-out 50-video human RSM. Model fit was evaluated with 10-fold cross-validation over stimulus pairs (5 repeats) as the squared Spearman correlation between out-of-fold predictions and observed similarities. Because the predictors are fixed stimulus properties and only one weight per predictor is estimated, pair-level folds do not fit stimulus-specific parameters. Unique variance for a predictor set was the full-model r 2 minus the r 2 of the model without that set; shared variance was the remainder. Significance was assessed by permuting the video labels of the human RSM (1,000 permutations) and Bonferronicorrecting across two families: pre-labeled annotations and 8 summary tests (model totals and variance-partition terms) in Fig. 2. Confidence intervals were obtained by a video-level bootstrap: on each of 1,000 iterations the 50 test videos were resampled with replacement, pairs of a video with itself were discarded, and all models were refit with the same cross-validation, with folds grouped by original video pair so that duplicated pairs never appeared in both training and test folds. Intervals are 2.5th-97.5th percentiles.

4.6 Visual and caption analysis

To interpret the learned dimensions, we examined how video examples were distributed across the embedding. For each of the top 11 dimensions, we selected the eight videos with the highest activations in each dimension and visually and semantically identified common themes.

We also analyzed the video captions within dimensions. For each dimension, we compared caption word frequencies between the 8 highest and 8 lowest loading videos. Each word was scored with a smoothed log ratio, log (︁ (n high + 0.5)/(n low + 0.5) )︁ , weighted by log(n high + n low + 1) to down-weight rare words. The top 20 words with positive log ratios were retained and reported as word clouds with font-size scaled by log ratio, for each dimension to aid interpretation and labeling.

We additionally calculated Jensen-Shannon divergence (bits) between the full caption word distributions of the 8 highest and 8 lowest loading videos, averaged over 200 random tie-breaks. Significance was assessed against a null of 5,000 random disjoint 8-video pairs (mean 0.61 bits).

4.7 Neural comparisons

We also compared fMRI data from a separate group of 4 healthy young adults. These data were collected in a previous study [12] ; all participants provided written informed consent, and the study was approved by the Johns Hopkins University Institutional Review Board. During scanning, participants viewed all 250 video clips in random order across multiple runs using a rapid event-related design, with each clip repeated 9-10 times for the 200 training clips and 18-20 times for the 50 test clips. Regions of interest (ROIs) were defined anatomically and supplemented with functional localizers of the lateral stream: EVC, MT, LOC, EBA, pSTS, and aSTS.

We performed whole-brain searchlight RSA using a 3-voxel radius sphere centered on each reliable voxel. For each searchlight sphere, we constructed a local neural RSM from the Pearson correlation distances between the 50 test stimuli. We evaluated two complementary searchlight analyses:

Multiple regression RSA.

Within each sphere, we regressed the local neural RSM onto two predictor sets in separate models: the 40 learned dimensions (and 11 in a supplemental experiment) and 13 pre-labeled annotations (12 behavioral and 1 action category). Each model was fit with 10-fold cross-validation over the 50 test stimuli. We computed cross-validated Spearman correlation squared (r 2 ) with the observed local RSM. This produced, for every sphere, a full-model r 2 (all predictors jointly) and a unique r 2 for each individual predictor, computed as the difference between the full model and a model omitting that predictor (r 2 full -r 2 leave-one-out ). Per subject, we visualized the combined full-model map on that subject's own native FreeSurfer inflated surface.

Winner-take-all.

Within each searchlight sphere, we computed the Spearman correlation between the local neural RSM and the similarity vector of each of the top 11 learned dimensions individually (marginal r). Each voxel was assigned the label of the dimension with the highest r, and voxels where no dimension exceeded r > 0.1 were left unlabeled. Voxelwise maps were projected onto each subject's FreeSurfer inflated cortical surface, and surface faces were colored by the majority label of their vertices.

In addition, for each ROI localizer, neural RSMs were constructed by computing Pearson correlation between voxel patterns for each pair of videos. Using a similar multiple regression RSA approach as before, we predicted the upper triangle of each neural RSM using the pre-labeled annotations and learned dimensions and compared using Spearman rank correlation squared (r 2 ). The noise ceiling was calculated using the method described in Nili et al [36] . The lower bound is the mean Spearman r 2 between each subject's RSM and the mean of the other subjects (leave-one-out); the upper bound is the mean Spearman r 2 between each subject's RSM and the mean of all subjects (including themselves).

4.8 Dimension recoverability

To evaluate the stability of the embedding dimensions, we retrained the model 20 times under two perturbations: random re-initialization (seed) on the same triplets and retraining on triplets resampled with replacement to the same size (bootstrap). Following the procedure of Hebart et al. [17] : each reference dimension was matched to whichever retrained column correlated most highly with it. The correlations across dimensions were Fisher z-transformed, averaged, and back-transformed to a mean reliability, separately for seed and bootstrap retrains. Dimensions were considered recoverable if they surpassed a threshold value of r = 0.6-the threshold Hebart et al. used to report dimension reliability. To confirm this threshold is not attributable to chance given the limited number of candidate columns per retrain (40 pruned dimensions), we built a null distribution by shuffling each reference dimension's video correspondence before matching (500 permutations); the null mean reliability never exceeded r = 0.26, confirming this threshold is far above chance.

Fractionation reproducibility was measured on independent retrains of the embedding. For each of the 20 bootstrap retrains, we selected 11 dimensions from that retrain's own embedding using the same greedy forward cumulative approach described above. Each selected dimension was matched to its closest-correlating (Pearson r) reported dimension across all 250 videos. A reported dimension was classified as fractionated in a given retrain when two or more of that retrain's selected dimensions matched it above a floor of 0.3 (99.7th percentile of permutation null). For each classified pair we computed shared top-20 videos, shared top-10 contrastive caption words, and Pearson r, and retained only pairs closer to the reported caregiving/infantplay example (r = 0.76, 3/20, 3/10) than to a true-merge control (r = 1.0, 20/20, 10/10)-shared videos ≤ 11, shared words ≤ 6, r < 0.8.

4.9 Statistics and reproducibility

This study was not preregistered. Sample size was not determined by a power analysis; instead, the number of triplets was fixed in advance by the pairwise coverage criterion described in Section 4.2, which ensured every video pair co-occurred in at least one triplet (∼4 judgments per pair for the 250-video training set, 215 participants; ∼9 per pair for the 50-video test set, 17 participants). The number of participants followed from the number of triplets required, given that each participant completed at least 220 trials. Data availability.

The triplet odd-one-out similarity judgments collected in this study (training and validation set: 49,484 triplets from 215 participants; held-out test set: 3,739 triplets from 17 participants), the learned 40-dimensional embedding, and the video caption data are publicly available at https://github.com/garciakathy/similarity-judgments-data-driven [37] . All participant data are de-identified. The video stimuli are drawn from the Moments in Time dataset [5] and are available from its creators under their terms of use. The pre-labeled behavioral annotations and fMRI data were previously published by McMahon et al. [12] and are available at https://osf.io/4j29y/ [38].

Code availability.

All code used to train the sparse positive similarity embedding and to perform the multiple regression RSA, searchlight, dimension recoverability, and caption analyses is publicly available at https://github.com/garciakathy/similarity-judgments-data-driven [37].

Competing interests.

The authors declare no competing interests.

Author contributions. K.G. and L.I. conceived the study. K.G. designed and collected the behavioral experiments, performed the analyses, and wrote the original draft. L.I. supervised the project and acquired funding. Both authors edited the manuscript.

held-out similarity judgments (Spearman-Brown corrected split half r² = 0.67) and by the stability of the learned dimensions across bootstrap and random-seed retrains (Section 4.8).

The fMRI dataset [12] uses a dense-sampling design: a small number of participants (n = 4) each viewed every video many times (9-10 repetitions per training video, 18-20 per test video), which supports reliable within-subject estimates of neural representational geometry. All neural analyses were therefore performed and reported separately for each participant, and the learned dimensions explained more variance than the prelabeled annotations across occipitotemporal cortex in all four participants (Extended Data Fig. 6).

Exclusion criteria for the behavioral experiments (attention-check accuracy; Section 4.2) were established before data analysis. Participants were not assigned to experimental groups, so randomization and blinding were not applicable; trial order and the on-screen arrangement of videos within each triplet were randomized. Gray shaded regions show the noise ceiling. [36] The lower bound is the mean Spearman r 2 between each subject's RSM and the mean of the other subjects (leave-one-out). The upper bound is the mean Spearman r 2 between each subject's RSM and the mean of all subjects.

Fig 1

Fig 1 Methods overview. (a) We collected a new dataset of triplet judgments from 250 3-second videos of everyday 2-person events. Participants were asked to select "which video was the odd one out?" Two experiments were conducted, the first to collect the training and validation set of triplets (49,484) and later to collect a held-out set of test triplets (3,739). (b) A SPoSE model was trained on a training set of triplets, to make a prediction of the odd one out. This prediction was compared to the human choice and model weights were updated (see Methods, Section 4.3). (c) Pre-labeled annotations released with the dataset were converted into RSMs and compared to the similarity probability matrix using multiple regression RSA.

Fig 2

Fig 2 Predicting similarity judgments with pre-labeled annotations and learned dimensions. (a) Total variance explained by each pre-labeled annotation individually in a multipleregression RSA, alongside the total explained by all 13 annotations jointly (rightmost bar). (b) Total variance explained by all 40 learned dimensions, and by the top 11 dimensions. (c) Combined model of the pre-labeled annotations and the 40 learned dimensions, decomposed into variance unique to each set and variance shared between them; the square marker denotes the total of the combined model, with its 95% CI shown beside the bar. Error bars show 95% confidence intervals from a video-level bootstrap (1,000 resamples of the 50 test videos). Dashed gray line: split-half reliability of the heldout human judgments (Spearman-Brown corrected), used as a noise ceiling; the shaded band is its 95% CI. Asterisks indicate p ≤ 0.05 by permutation test (1,000 permutations), Bonferroni-corrected.

Fig 3

Fig.3Interpreting learned dimensions. The top 11 dimensions that explain the most cumulative variance in similarity judgments, illustrated with their most strongly associated stimuli. Each row represents a dimension, with rows sorted by greedy predictive performance (Methods, Section 4.3), and the columns show a frame from each of the 8 videos with the highest activations on that dimension. Next to each dimension is a word cloud of the 20 most contrastive words from human-written captions of those 8 videos, colored by part of speech: noun (blue), verb (green), adjective (red), adverb (purple) and other (gray). Word size is scaled by contrastive log ratio, with larger words being more contrastive.

Fig 4

Fig 4 Relationship between leading learned dimensions and pre-labeled scene/social annotations. We correlated each of the top eleven learned dimensions with pre-labeled annotations (see Extended Data Fig 5 for all learned dimensions). Colorbar indicates correlation (Spearman r) value, asterisks represent significant correlations (p ≤ 0.05, Bonferroni corrected across the 13 annotations within each dimension).

Fig 5

Fig 5 Aligning pre-labeled annotations and learned dimensions with fMRI data. Results from a wholebrain searchlight multiple regression RSA in one representative subject (see other Subjects' results in Extended Data Fig 6). Voxelwise explained variance (Spearman r 2 ) of neural RSA from (a) 13 pre-labeled annotations and (b) 40 learned embedding dimensions. Both models were evaluated using 10-fold cross-validated regression RSA with identical searchlight parameters. Colorbars are matched across panels to enable direct comparison. Views shown: lateral, medial, and ventral surfaces for each hemisphere. Only voxels exceeding r 2 > 0.01 are displayed; values above the 99th percentile are clipped.
